These early life stages are critically sensitive to thermal conditions, with even slight deviations from 12 °C [T = 12 °C] dramatically affecting yolk absorption efficiency and swim bladder inflation success. Field observations indicate that the narrow thermal window during this endotrophic phase imposes strong selection on spawning site selection, as females must deposit their adhesive eggs in shallows where temperature stability persists through the incubation period.

Juvenile Fringebarbel Sturgeon exhibit a protracted growth trajectory that continues well into their second decade of life, a pattern typical of large-bodied acipenserids. The ultimate total length attained by adults reaches 211.0 centimeters [Li = 211.0 centimeters], a formidable size that places Acipenser nudiventris among the larger members of its genus. Historical commercial catch records from the Caspian Sea during the mid-twentieth century documented individuals approaching this asymptotic mass with regularity, though contemporary populations rarely exhibit such dimensions due to size-selective fishing pressure. The energetic demands of achieving this adult body size are met through a benthic, predominantly piscivorous diet, with larger specimens also consuming molluscs and crustaceans when available.

Reproductive output in the Fringebarbel Sturgeon is remarkably high, reflecting the species' evolutionary strategy as an iteroparous spawner with high fecundity. This daily rate, sustained over the several-day spawning period, results in a total clutch that can exceed several hundred thousand eggs annually. This relatively low reproductive frequency is compensated by the sheer magnitude of daily egg production, ensuring that even infrequent spawners contribute substantial offspring to the next generation.

Sexual maturation in Acipenser nudiventris is a notably slow process, with individuals reaching puberty only after many years of somatic growth. The age at first reproduction has been documented at 5475 days after hatching [tR = 5475 days after hatching] when reared under average spring temperatures of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding activity is a consequence of the species' protracted juvenile phase, during which individuals must accumulate sufficient lipid stores and attain the minimum body size required for successful gonadal development. Comparative studies with the closely related Russian sturgeon (Acipenser gueldenstaedtii) suggest that this age at first spawning may vary latitudinally, with populations in cooler northern reaches of the Caspian basin potentially delaying reproduction by an additional year or two. Longevity in sturgeons is legendary, and the Fringebarbel Sturgeon is no exception, with a documented maximum lifespan of 13140 days [am = 13140 days] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], equivalent to approximately 36 years. This extended life span is a hallmark of the genus Acipenser, whose members typically exhibit slow senescence rates and maintain reproductive viability into advanced age. The extreme longevity of A. nudiventris likely evolved as a bet-hedging strategy in response to the high interannual variability in spawning success caused by fluctuating river flows and unpredictable food availability in the Caspian Sea ecosystem. Physiological death in these fish is rarely attributable to senescence alone; instead, most natural mortality events are linked to the energetic exhaustion following repeated spawning migrations, particularly among older individuals whose metabolic efficiency declines with age. Captive records from the Ural Sturgeon Hatchery confirm that individuals can survive well beyond five decades under protected conditions, though wild populations face substantial mortality from anthropogenic factors before reaching their physiological maximum.
